title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
gist: Binance says a months-long North Korean-attributed campaign using fake recruitment interviews, zero-day malware, a compromised internal AI tool and EIP-7702 abuse targeted $6.34 billion, of which $2.85 billion was frozen. The incident is the largest crypto theft attempt on record.

insights.claim: The heist targeted $6.34 billion from Binance wallets, the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft, with $2.85 billion frozen or intercepted so far.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Net loss is roughly $3.5 billion before recoveries; Binance says it has set aside funds to cover it.

insights.claim: The FBI and TRM Security attribute the heist to North Korean actors, and TRM tracks the group as TraderTraitor.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: State-sponsored theft continues to scale and fund North Korea, increasing sanctions and regulatory pressure on exchanges.

insights.claim: Binance says the campaign ran from no later than June until last Thursday, when attackers compromised an engineer's laptop and withdrew assets, and was a sophisticated multi-stage operation, not a single breach or simple phishing.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Long dwell time shows detection and response gaps even at the largest exchange.
insights.quote: It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.

insights.claim: The first incident likely occurred in June when an engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew; Binance's security team detected the compromised laptop only after the operators learned engineers' roles on the wallet infrastructure team.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Software supply-chain compromises give attackers reconnaissance before detection.

insights.claim: In September an engineer was lured via a legitimate job-hunting platform into fake interviews with a supposed HR rep and CEO, then told to download an 'assignment' from a repository whose malicious code ran during setup.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Social engineering against developers is a primary vector against crypto custody.

insights.claim: The 0-day malware replaced a legitimate development tool component, evaded endpoint security tools and concealed its traces, per Binance.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Endpoint security alone failed against a tailored zero-day.

insights.claim: On October 20 the attackers used the compromised engineer's computer and an internal AI tool to take control of two other engineer devices, one holding a token granting access to a container deployment.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Internal AI tooling became an attack path for lateral movement, a new enterprise risk.

insights.claim: Nine days later the attacker used the stolen credential on the third engineer's device to deploy a container and run a script that initiated transfers, extending access to an internal wallet signing service to bypass normal withdrawal processes.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Compromise of the signing service allowed transactions outside normal withdrawal controls.

insights.claim: Binance hot wallets sent about 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP, and then 18,270 BTC, to attacker-controlled addresses.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Shows scale and multi-chain breadth of the drained assets.

insights.claim: The attacker used the signing service to exploit Ethereum's EIP-7702 delegation mechanism, giving an attacker-controlled smart contract partial execution rights over a Binance hot wallet, with 50 signing transactions used to manipulate the account nonce.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: EIP-7702 delegation creates a persistent on-chain permission risk beyond exchange-level withdrawal controls.

insights.claim: Suspending withdrawals and shutting down hot wallet services did not invalidate the on-chain EIP-7702 authorizations, and because the hot wallet used MPC there was no single private key to revoke them, so Binance needed a specialized procedure and extra time.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: MPC wallet designs complicate emergency revocation, a design trade-off for custodians.
insights.quote: suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorized asset movements.

insights.claim: TRM says the attackers laundered stolen assets through TRON and Ethereum using a self-minted token and liquidity pool, a lending receipt token passed between wallets, and cross-chain swaps chained through two bridges.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Laundering through DeFi and bridges challenges freezing and tracing efforts.
